title: Supervisor hazard, information, and instruction duties
mainQuestion: What specific hazard, information, and instruction duties does a supervisor owe to employees under the supervisor's supervision and direction?
studySummary: A supervisor's subsection 9.1(2) duties add specific employee-facing requirements without limiting the general duties in subsection 9.1(1). The supervisor must acquaint supervised employees with hazards connected to listed workplace items or agents, provide information necessary for their health and safety, and provide instruction necessary for their health and safety.

objectives.objective: Recall the supervisor's duty to acquaint employees with hazards.
objectives.guidedQuestion: What hazards must a supervisor acquaint supervised employees with?
objectives.studyAnswer: Every supervisor shall acquaint employees under the supervisor's supervision and direction with any hazard connected with the use, handling, storage, disposal, and transport of any tool, equipment, machine, device, or biological, chemical, or physical agent.

objectives.objective: Recall the supervisor's duty to provide necessary health and safety information.
objectives.guidedQuestion: What information must a supervisor provide to supervised employees?
objectives.studyAnswer: Every supervisor shall provide the information necessary to ensure the health and safety of the employees under the supervisor's supervision and direction.

objectives.objective: Recall the supervisor's duty to provide necessary health and safety instruction.

objectives.studyAnswer: Every supervisor shall provide the instruction necessary to ensure the health and safety of the employees under the supervisor's supervision and direction.

provide the instruction that is necessary to ensure the health and safety of the employees under the supervisor’s supervision and direction.

title: Who may hold a conservation easement
mainQuestion: Which public bodies, non-profit corporations, and prescribed eligible persons may hold a conservation easement?
studySummary: Section 5 identifies who may hold a conservation easement. Current holder categories include provincial and federal Crown bodies and agencies, local governments and their agencies, qualifying non-profit corporations, and prescribed eligible persons, bodies, groups, or classes that may hold an interest in land. One paragraph is repealed and does not add a current holder category.

objectives.objective: Recall the public Crown and local-government holders.
objectives.guidedQuestion: Which Crown and local-government bodies may hold a conservation easement?
objectives.studyAnswer: A conservation easement may be held by the Crown in right of the Province or its agency, the Crown in right of Canada or its agency, or a local government or local-government agency.

objectives.objective: Recall the qualifying non-profit holder category.
objectives.guidedQuestion: What kind of non-profit corporation may hold a conservation easement?
objectives.studyAnswer: A non-profit corporation may hold a conservation easement if one of its primary purposes is a purpose mentioned in section 3.

evidence.evidenceText:

a non-profit corporation that has as one of its primary purposes a purpose mentioned in section 3;

objectives.objective: Recall the prescribed eligible private or group holder category.
objectives.guidedQuestion: What prescribed persons, bodies, or groups may hold a conservation easement?
objectives.studyAnswer: Any person, body, group, or class of persons, bodies, or groups may hold a conservation easement if eligible to hold an interest in land and prescribed by regulation for that paragraph.

any person, body or group or class of persons, bodies or groups eligible to hold an interest in land and prescribed by regulation for the purposes of this paragraph.

title: Permit for access to non-controlled-access highway
mainQuestion: When is a Minister's permit required for access to a highway that is not controlled access, and when may the Minister grant it?
studySummary: Section 39.1 controls access routes to highways that have not been designated controlled access highways. A person must not construct, use, or permit use of listed private or local-government access routes to such a highway without a Minister's permit. The Minister may grant the permit application if, in the Minister's opinion, the proposed access would not be inconsistent with established regulatory safety standards for that kind of highway access.

objectives.objective: Recall the access activities that require a permit.
objectives.guidedQuestion: What access to a non-controlled-access highway is prohibited without a Minister's permit?
objectives.studyAnswer: No person shall construct, use, or permit the use of a private road, entrance way, driveway, gate, or local government road or street intended for or capable of providing access to any part of a highway that has not been designated a controlled access highway without obtaining a permit from the Minister.

evidence.evidenceText: 39.1(1)No person shall construct, use or permit the use of any private road, entrance way, driveway or gate or any local government road or street intended for or capable of providing access to any part of a highway that has not been designated to be a controlled access highway without obtaining a permit from the Minister.

objectives.objective: Recall the condition for granting an access permit.
objectives.guidedQuestion: When may the Minister grant an application for a non-controlled-access highway access permit?
objectives.studyAnswer: The Minister may grant the application if the proposed access, in the Minister's opinion, would not be inconsistent with safety standards established by regulation respecting access to highways that have not been designated controlled access highways.

evidence.evidenceText: 39.1(2)The Minister may grant an application for a permit under subsection (1) if the proposed access, in the Minister’s opinion, would not be inconsistent with such safety standards as have been established by regulation respecting access to highways that have not been designated to be controlled access highways.

title: Professional reporting duty for notifiable disease, injury risk, or notifiable event
mainQuestion: Which professionals must report specified public-health concerns, what belief triggers the report, and how must the report be made?
studySummary: Section 27 imposes a reporting duty on medical practitioners, nurse practitioners, midwives, and nurses while providing professional services to certain people outside hospital or institutional settings. The duty arises when they have reasonable grounds to believe the person has or may have a listed disease-related condition, prescribed injury or risk factor, or prescribed notifiable event. The report must go to a medical officer of health or Minister-designated person and must be made in accordance with the regulations.

objectives.guidedQuestion: Who must make a section 27 report, and to whom is it reported?
objectives.studyAnswer: A medical practitioner, nurse practitioner, midwife, or nurse shall report to a medical officer of health or a person designated by the Minister when the subsection 27(1) conditions are met.

title: Digitally scanned image filing or registration of instruments
mainQuestion: When may a Land Titles Act instrument be filed or registered as a digitally scanned image, and what submission requirements apply?
studySummary: Section 17.11 permits filing or registration by digitally scanned image for instruments that may be filed or registered under the Act, subject to exceptions for required electronic instruments and regulatory exceptions. The scanned image must use an approved format equivalent when printed to the prescribed counterpart and must be submitted through Service New Brunswick technology. The subscriber or land surveyor must also provide satisfactory evidence of identity or authorization to the registrar.

objectives.objective: Recall when an instrument may be filed or registered by digitally scanned image.
objectives.guidedQuestion: Which Land Titles Act instruments may be filed or registered by submitting a digitally scanned image?
objectives.studyAnswer: Except for an instrument designated under subsection 17.1(1) that is required to be in electronic format, and except as otherwise provided in the regulations, an instrument that may be filed or registered under the Act may be filed or registered by submitting a digitally scanned image of the instrument.

evidence.evidenceText: 17.11(1)Except with respect to an instrument designated under subsection 17.1(1) that is required to be in electronic format, and except as otherwise provided in the regulations, an instrument that may be filed or registered under this Act may be filed or registered by submitting a digitally scanned image of the instrument.

objectives.objective: Recall the format and technology requirements for the scanned image.
objectives.guidedQuestion: What format and technology requirements apply to a digitally scanned image submitted for filing or registration?
objectives.studyAnswer: The digitally scanned image shall be in a format approved by the Registrar General as equivalent, when printed, in form and content to its counterpart prescribed by regulation, and it shall be submitted using the technology put in place by Service New Brunswick.

title: Personal Property Registry notice of household-goods order
mainQuestion: How does registration in the Personal Property Registry give notice of a household-goods order, and what exceptions limit that notice effect?
studySummary: Section 30 allows a spouse benefiting from a household-goods order under specified provisions to register a notice of the order in the Personal Property Registry. The registration may be renewed, discharged, or otherwise amended under Personal Property Security Act regulations. For subsection 29(2) notice purposes, registration is deemed notice of the order and its terms, but that deemed notice rule does not apply to certain serial-numbered goods unless serial-number-described or to lower-value consumer goods acquisitions within the stated sale or lease thresholds.

objectives.objective: Recall who may register notice of a household-goods order.
objectives.guidedQuestion: Who may register a notice of a household-goods order in the Personal Property Registry?
objectives.studyAnswer: A spouse in whose favour an order in respect of household goods is made under subsection 27(3) or paragraph 23(1)(d) may register a notice of the order in the Personal Property Registry in accordance with the regulations under the Personal Property Security Act.

evidence.evidenceText: 30(1)A spouse in whose favour an order in respect of household goods is made under subsection 27(3) or paragraph 23(1)(d) may register a notice of the order in the Personal Property Registry in accordance with the regulations under the Personal Property Security Act.

objectives.objective: Recall how a registration may be changed after it is made.
objectives.guidedQuestion: How may a registered notice of a household-goods order be changed?
objectives.studyAnswer: A registration of the notice may be renewed, discharged, or otherwise amended in accordance with the regulations under the Personal Property Security Act.

evidence.evidenceText: 30(2)A registration under subsection (1) may be renewed, discharged or otherwise amended in accordance with the regulations under the Personal Property Security Act.

objectives.objective: Recall the deemed notice effect of registration.
objectives.guidedQuestion: For subsection 29(2), what notice effect does registration of a household-goods order have?
objectives.studyAnswer: For determining under subsection 29(2) whether a person had notice that household goods were being disposed of in contravention of the order, registration of a notice of the order affecting the goods is deemed to be notice of the order and its terms to that person.

evidence.evidenceText: 30(3)For the purposes of determining under subsection 29(2) whether a person had notice that household goods were being disposed of in contravention of an order under subsection 27(3) or paragraph 23(1)(d), the registration under subsection (1) of a notice of an order affecting household goods shall be deemed to be notice of the order and its terms to that person.

objectives.studyAnswer: It does not apply to a disposition of serial numbered household goods unless the goods were described by serial number in the notice registration, or to a disposition of household goods acquired as consumer goods if the purchase price does not exceed $1,000 for a sale or the market value does not exceed $1,000 for a lease.

title: Compelled answers and limited later use in provincial proceedings
mainQuestion: How does section 7 require answers despite prosecution, penalty, or forfeiture exposure, and how does it limit later use of those answers?
studySummary: Section 7 applies in civil proceedings, trials for violations of provincial statutes, and prosecutions for penalties imposed by provincial law. A person is not excused from answering a question merely because the answer may tend to expose that person to prosecution, penalty, or forfeiture under provincial laws or certain federal statutes involving provincial-statute offences. Evidence so given is not usable or receivable against that person in another proceeding, except a prosecution for perjury in giving that evidence.

objectives.objective: Recall the proceedings in which section 7 compellability applies.
objectives.guidedQuestion: In what proceedings does section 7 say a person is not excused from answering?
objectives.studyAnswer: The rule applies in any civil proceeding, on the trial of a person in any court for violation of a statute of the Province, and on a prosecution in any court for any penalty imposed by a law of the Province.

evidence.evidenceText: 7In any civil proceeding, as well as upon the trial of a person in any court for a violation of a statute of this Province, or upon a prosecution in any court for any penalty imposed by a law of this Province, no person shall be excused from answering any question

objectives.objective: Recall why possible liability does not excuse answering.
objectives.guidedQuestion: What possible liability is not a ground for refusing to answer under section 7?
objectives.studyAnswer: A person is not excused from answering on the ground that the answer may tend to render that person liable to a prosecution, penalty, or forfeiture under the laws of the Province or under a Canadian statute that makes it an offence to violate a provincial statute.

evidence.evidenceText: upon the ground that the answer to such question may tend to render him liable to a prosecution, penalty or forfeiture under the laws of this Province, or under any statute of Canada, whereby it is made an offence to violate any provincial statute;

objectives.objective: Recall the later-use protection and perjury exception.
objectives.guidedQuestion: How may evidence given under section 7 be used against the person later?
objectives.studyAnswer: Evidence so given shall not be used or received in evidence against that person in any proceeding instituted against the person, except in a prosecution for perjury in giving that evidence.

title: Registering extra-provincial court will materials affecting land
mainQuestion: What extra-provincial court will materials affecting New Brunswick land may be registered, and what effect do they have when registered?
studySummary: Subsection 23(1), subject to subsection 23(2), deals with a will affecting land or an interest in land in the Province when the original will is deposited in a court outside the Province. A certified copy, probate, letters of administration with the will annexed, or an exemplification of probate or letters may be treated as evidence that the original will is deposited in that court if it bears the required court officer hand and seal and the seal is proven and authenticated as described. Once those materials are registered in a county registry office as other conveyances are registered, they have the same effect as if the original will had been registered there.

objectives.objective: Recall when the extra-provincial court will-registration rule applies.
objectives.guidedQuestion: What kind of will deposit brings subsection 23(1) into play?
objectives.studyAnswer: Subject to subsection 23(2), subsection 23(1) applies where a will affecting land in the Province, or an interest in that land, is deposited in a court outside the Province.

evidence.evidenceText: 23(1)Subject to subsection (2), where a will affecting land in this Province, or any interest therein, is deposited in any court out of this Province

objectives.objective: Recall which court-certified will materials may evidence the original will deposit.
objectives.guidedQuestion: Which extra-provincial court materials may be deemed evidence that the original will is deposited in that court?
objectives.studyAnswer: A certified copy of the will, the probate of the will, letters of administration with the will annexed, or an exemplification of the probate or letters may be deemed evidence of the original will being deposited in the court, if they purport to be under the hand of the officer having custody of the court records and the court seal, with the seal proven and authenticated as required.

evidence.evidenceText: a certified copy thereof, the probate of such will, or any letters of administration with the will annexed, purporting to be under the hand of the officer having the custody of the records of the court in which the original will was deposited and of the seal of the said court, or an exemplification of such probate or letters of administration with the will annexed, purporting to be certified under the hand of the officer having the custody of the records of the court in which the original will was deposited and of the seal of such court, and the seal affixed to such certified copy, probate or exemplification thereof, or to such letters of administration with the will annexed, being proven before any of the persons authorized by the laws of this Province to take acknowledgement or proof of deeds affecting land in this Province, and authenticated in a like manner, shall be deemed to be evidence of the said original will being deposited in such court;
